Maricopa County by the numbers

Which Maricopa County offices handle property tax?

The county splits the job between an assessor and a treasurer. The Maricopa County Assessor values property, classifies it and mails the annual Notice of Value. The Maricopa County Treasurer bills and collects real and personal property taxes for more than 1,800 tax districts, including the state, county, cities and towns, schools, community colleges and special districts, then distributes the money to them.

  • Treasurer: 301 West Jefferson Street, Suite 100, Phoenix, AZ 85003. Office hours 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Customer service 602-506-8511.
  • Assessor: 602-506-3406.
  • Parcel search and online payment run through the Treasurer's site, and the eNotices program offers paperless bills with an authorization code printed on your tax bill.

The Treasurer's site warns about mail, text and phone scams that push alternate payment methods. Pay only through the county's own site or the address on your bill.

What is Maricopa County like for a home seller?

Maricopa County is the biggest county in Arizona by a wide margin. It covers 9,224 square miles, stretching 132 miles west to east, and had 4,420,568 people in the 2020 census, about 62% of the state. The 2020 count also showed 1,812,827 housing units with 9.3% vacant, and 63.0% of occupied homes were owner-occupied. Phoenix is the seat, and the county holds fifteen cities and ten towns, including Mesa, Chandler, Scottsdale, Tempe and Gilbert.

The county also contains a mix of school districts, from unified districts such as Mesa, Chandler, Gilbert and Scottsdale to union high school and elementary districts in Phoenix and the West Valley. Because each district, city, fire district and special district levies its own rate, two houses with the same value can carry different bills. Look up your parcel rather than relying on a neighbor's number.

Five Indian reservations lie inside the county, the largest being the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community and the Gila River Indian Community.

When is Maricopa County property tax due?

Under A.R.S. 42-18052, half the tax is due October 1 and the other half the following March 1. Unpaid halves become delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and May 1. A bill of $100 or less is due in full on October 1 and is delinquent after December 31. If a delinquency date lands on a weekend or holiday, it moves to the next business day.

May 1, 2027 is a Saturday, so under subsection D the delinquency time moves to 5:00 p.m. on the next business day. Paying the full year on or before December 31 avoids interest under A.R.S. 42-18053. Otherwise unpaid tax bears 16% a year, simple, and a part of a month counts as a whole month.

How does the Maricopa County tax lien process work?

The Treasurer publishes an annual calendar for delinquent accounts. Delinquent taxes are assessed an advertising fee in January, and an online tax lien auction takes place in February. Late in the spring a second-half bill goes delinquent on May 1, and first delinquent notices go out in June. Bidders may begin buying the current delinquent year after that. A second round of delinquent notices goes out in December.

Buyers at the sale hold certificates of purchase, and the Treasurer's calendar lists December 31 as the final day to purchase subsequent taxes and assignments. For a seller the message is simple: do not let the first half sit unpaid into the new year.

The lien itself comes from A.R.S. 42-17153. It attaches on January 1 of the tax year, ranks ahead of other liens except state liens and liens for taxes of other years, and stays until the tax, interest and charges are paid, title vests in a purchaser at a tax sale, or a certificate of removal and abatement issues. A title company will want the lien cleared from your sale proceeds.

How do you appeal a Maricopa County property value?

The Assessor must mail a Notice of Value between January 1 and March 1 each year. If you think the full cash value or the legal class is wrong, file a Petition for Review of Real Property Valuation with the Assessor within 60 days after the mailing date. Owners or their representatives can file online. The Assessor's handout also says the appeal covers full cash value and classification, not the limited property value.

  • Assessor level: the Assessor must answer all appeals by August 15 in the handout's example year. The 2026 notice went out February 21, 2025, with an April 22, 2025 filing deadline.
  • State Board of Equalization: file within 25 days of the Assessor's decision. The board hears both sides before an officer.
  • Superior Court: tax court or small claims, filed by December 15 of the notice year, or within 60 days of the latest administrative decision. Small claims covers owner-occupied residential property and any property valued under $2 million.

The handout explains that limited property value is the only value used to compute tax and rises at most 5% a year unless the property changes through additions, deletions or a change in use. A new owner who acquires a house after December 15 can appeal to court if the prior owner did not appeal that year's value. The statutory 60-day rule is in A.R.S. 42-16051.

What relief programs does the Maricopa County Assessor offer?

The Assessor's homepage lists veteran personal exemptions for the 100% service-connected disability exemption, and a notice dated June 24, 2026 says changes to the disabled veterans' exemptions arrive in 2027 as part of the state budget. A September 21, 2026 article summarizes legislative changes from the 2026 session that affect owners and veterans. Read those pages before you rely on an older rule.

The office also takes rental registrations online and holds virtual appointments. For widow, widower, disability and senior-valuation programs, ask the Assessor for current forms, dollar limits and deadlines.

What happens to tax when you sell a Maricopa County house?

The deed gets recorded and the Assessor updates ownership, but the lien for the current tax year already exists from January 1. At closing, the title company gets the amount owed from the Treasurer and pays it from your proceeds. If you sell in the fall, it matters whether the first half was paid. If a delinquent half is still unpaid at closing, interest at 16% a year has been counted from its delinquency date.

Foreclosure sales that bring in more than the debt can leave money behind. Maricopa County's Treasurer lists excess proceeds that a foreclosing attorney deposited under A.R.S. 33-812 on the Treasurer's website.

When is the Maricopa County property tax deadline in 2026?

The first half of 2026 tax was due October 1 and became delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 2, 2026. Full-year 2026 taxes over $100 can still be paid without interest through December 31, 2026. The second half is due March 1, 2027.

How much interest does Maricopa County charge on late property tax?

Delinquent tax bears 16% interest a year, simple, from the delinquency date, and a fraction of a month counts as a whole month, under A.R.S. 42-18053. No interest is collected if the full year is paid by December 31 or if the delinquency came from an assessor or treasurer error.

How long do I have to appeal my Maricopa County Notice of Value?

You have 60 days after the Assessor mailed the notice. File a Petition for Review of Real Property Valuation with the Assessor, online or on paper. If you disagree with the result, the State Board of Equalization takes appeals within 25 days of the Assessor's decision.

Who do I call about my Maricopa County property tax bill?

Call the Treasurer's customer service at 602-506-8511 for amounts due and payments. Call the Assessor at 602-506-3406 about value, classification and exemptions. The Treasurer's office is at 301 West Jefferson Street, Suite 100, Phoenix, and is open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Can I sell my Maricopa County house if I owe property tax?

Yes. The tax is a lien that attaches on January 1 and is paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure for your closing date, because interest keeps accruing on delinquent halves until they are paid.

Pima County by the numbers

Which Pima County offices handle property tax?

Two county offices share the work, and both are in Tucson. The Pima County Assessor values and classifies property, takes appeals and runs the valuation relief programs. The Pima County Treasurer mails the statements, collects payments and sells tax liens on delinquent accounts. The Treasurer cannot change the amount of a bill unless the Board of Supervisors directs it, so a disagreement over value starts with the Assessor.

  • Treasurer: 240 N. Stone Avenue, lower level of the Pima County Public Service Center, Tucson, AZ 85701. Open Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., phone (520) 724-8341.
  • Assessor: 240 N Stone Ave, Tucson, AZ 85701, phone (520) 724-8630, with the Valuation Relief team at (520) 724-7500.

The Treasurer's office also keeps a holiday calendar. It closes November 26 and 27 for Thanksgiving, December 25, and January 1 and 18, 2027.

When are Pima County property taxes due and when are they late?

The first half is due October 1 and the second half March 1, with delinquency after 5:00 p.m. on the following November 1 and May 1 (A.R.S. 42-18052). The Treasurer mails statements in mid-September, and that is the only statement you receive unless the account goes delinquent. Delinquent real property notices go out in August and January.

For the 2026 tax year, the Treasurer's calendar lists December 31, 2026 as the full-year payment date. The second half is due March 1, 2027, and payments must be postmarked no later than May 3, 2027, because May 1 is a Saturday. Interest is not collected when the full-year tax is paid on or before December 31 of the tax year (A.R.S. 42-18053), so a bill that is still open today can be settled in full by the end of the year.

What happens to a delinquent Pima County tax bill?

Interest at 16 percent per year, simple, starts at delinquency, and a fraction of a month counts as a whole month. The Treasurer adds that taxes not paid before January of the following year pick up an additional $5.00 or 5 percent penalty. In February the delinquent lien is offered at the Treasurer's tax lien sale, held during the last week of the month, with no bidding on Tuesday because the Board of Supervisors meets that day.

At the sale the buyer purchases the lien on your taxes. After three years from the sale date, that buyer can foreclose on the lien and acquire the property. The details matter if you are thinking of selling.

  • The Treasurer cannot accept partial payments once a lien has been sold. All delinquent taxes, interest, penalties and fees must be paid in full.
  • Before a sale, the minimum payment is the tax, interest and fees for a delinquent installment, meaning one half-year.
  • The state statute lets a lien be sold for the combined delinquent taxes on a parcel, not just one year (A.R.S. 42-18104).

How can you pay the Pima County Treasurer?

You can pay online, by mail, or in person. Online payment is by ACH or electronic check, and the minimum payment is the greater of $10 or 10 percent of the installment due. The Treasurer says the online convenience fee goes entirely to the payment servicer.

  • Mail: send the coupon with a check, cashier's check or money order in US funds to PO Box 29011, Phoenix, AZ 85038-9011. Put your state code or reference number on the check, and do not mail cash.
  • In person: cash, check and card payments at the Treasurer's counter. Credit and debit cards carry a 2 percent service fee.
  • Wire: call (520) 724-8341 first.

Mortgage and tax service companies receive tax statement information on request, so a lender that escrows your taxes should have the bill. Property tax liability covers the calendar year, from January through December, even though the second installment falls due in the next calendar year.

How is a Pima County tax bill calculated?

The bill is the limited value times the assessment ratio times the combined tax rate, divided by $100. Primary and secondary taxes are figured the same way and added together. The Treasurer explains that primary taxes pay a jurisdiction's operating expenses and apply to the limited cash value, while secondary taxes pay for special districts such as fire districts and voter-approved bonds and budget overrides.

Your rate combines every jurisdiction taxing your address, for example the City of Tucson, Pima County and your school district. Two items on the bill are worth knowing.

  • Primary Tax Reduction: a credit on the school district's primary levy for owner-occupied homes, sometimes called the homeowner's rebate. The state reimburses the school district for eligible amounts.
  • Fire District Assistance: a countywide tax on every taxable property that supplements fire districts, levied under A.R.S. 48-807.

The Assessor stresses that it has no control over tax levies or rates. If you think your rate is too high, contact the political subdivisions listed on your bill.

How do you appeal a Pima County valuation?

File a petition with the Assessor within 60 days after the mail date of the Notice of Value (A.R.S. 42-16051). The Assessor says Notices of Value are mailed on or before March 1, and a Notice of Change that mails on or before September 30 has its own supplemental appeal. An assessment appeal tries to show the property was improperly valued, listed with the wrong class, or given an incorrectly calculated limited value. It is not a complaint about higher taxes.

The petition has to state a valuation method with supporting data.

  • Market approach: include the sale price of at least one comparable property in the same area, or the sale of your own property.
  • Replacement cost approach: include the cost to build or rebuild plus the land value.
  • Income approach: include the information required by A.R.S. 42-16052.

A Notice of Claim covers a factual error, and a Notice of Proposed Correction can arrive by certified mail at any time of year. The Treasurer advises paying the tax as billed while an appeal is pending. If a correction lowers the tax, you get a refund of the overpayment plus interest at the rate set by the Arizona Department of Revenue. If it raises the tax, you get 60 days to pay the increase without interest.

What relief and exemptions does Pima County offer?

The Assessor's Valuation Relief programs either reduce or freeze the limited assessed value for qualifying owners. Each program has strict statutory eligibility rules for the applicant and the household. The annual filing deadline is March 1, and later applications must include a Redemption Waiver form under A.R.S. 42-11153.

The Assessor currently highlights the exemption for a veteran with a 100 percent service-connected disability. Governor Hobbs signed H.B. 2792 on February 12, 2026, clarifying A.R.S. 42-11111 as an emergency measure effective for tax year 2026 and after. The veteran must be honorably discharged, hold a VA benefit summary letter confirming the 100 percent rating, and meet the income limit. The exemption covers one primary residence. Call (520) 724-7500 or write to ASRValRelief@pima.gov for current forms.

What size is Pima County, and what does that mean for sellers?

Pima County spans 9,189 square miles in south central Arizona, with Tucson as seat and largest city. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 1,074,685 residents. The county has two cities, Tucson and South Tucson, and the towns of Marana, Oro Valley and Sahuarita, plus unincorporated communities such as Casas Adobes and Catalina Foothills.

Census figures for 2020 to 2024 show 65.2 percent owner-occupied housing, a median owner-occupied value of $319,700 and median gross rent of $1,212. If you sell with taxes open, ask the title company for a payoff that includes interest through the closing date, and ask the Treasurer whether a lien has already been sold on the parcel.

More questions about Pima County, AZ Property Tax Guide

When are Pima County property taxes due?

October 1 for the first half and March 1 for the second half. They become delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and May 1. For 2026 the full year is due December 31, 2026, and second-half payments must be postmarked by May 3, 2027.

What interest does Pima County charge on late taxes?

Sixteen percent per year, simple, from the delinquency date, with a partial month counted as a whole month. The Treasurer also adds $5.00 or 5 percent for taxes unpaid into January. No interest is collected if the full year is paid by December 31.

What is the Pima County tax lien sale?

The Treasurer sells the lien for delinquent taxes during the last week of February. The house stays with the owner until the lien purchaser forecloses, which the purchaser may do after three years from the sale date.

Can I pay my Pima County property tax online?

Yes. The Treasurer takes ACH or electronic check payments online with a minimum of the greater of $10 or 10 percent of the installment. You can also mail a check to PO Box 29011, Phoenix, AZ 85038-9011, or pay in person at 240 N. Stone Avenue in Tucson.

Who do I call if my Pima County valuation looks wrong?

Call the Assessor at (520) 724-8630. The Treasurer cannot change a bill unless the Board of Supervisors directs it. File a petition within 60 days of the Notice of Value mail date, and keep paying the bill as issued while the appeal proceeds.

Who sends the property tax bill in Pinal County, Arizona?

The Pinal County Treasurer bills and collects property tax, and the Pinal County Assessor sets the values the bill is built on. The Treasurer also distributes the money to the school districts, fire districts, cities and towns, and the community college that levy on your parcel, so one county bill covers all of them.

The two offices sit in different buildings and answer different questions. Ask the Assessor about value, legal class, mailing address and exemptions. Ask the Treasurer about what you owe, how to pay and what happens when a payment is late. Arizona law does not require the Treasurer to mail a bill, so a missing statement does not excuse a missed due date.

Pinal County is a large county in central Arizona, about 5,366 square miles of land, and the county seat is Florence. It was cut out of Maricopa and Pima counties on February 1, 1875. Its five cities are Maricopa, Casa Grande, Apache Junction, Eloy and Coolidge. Towns include Florence, Kearny, Mammoth, Superior, Hayden and Queen Creek (mostly in Maricopa County), and San Tan Valley is the largest community by population. Parts of the Tohono O’odham Nation, the Gila River Indian Community and the San Carlos Apache Reservation lie inside the county, and the Ak-Chin Indian Community lies entirely inside it.

When are Pinal County property taxes due, and what does a late payment cost?

Bills of more than $100 are paid in two halves: the first half is due October 1 and the second half is due March 1. A half becomes delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 1 and May 1 respectively. If a delinquency date lands on a weekend or holiday, the cutoff moves to 5 p.m. on the next business day. The Treasurer measures these times against the Florence office hours, and satellite offices may be closed.

A bill of $100 or less is due in full on October 1 and is delinquent after December 31. Paying the whole year by December 31 keeps interest off the first half, under ARS 42-18053. Once a half is delinquent, interest runs at 16 percent a year, simple, and a part of a month counts as a full month. The Treasurer lists the monthly proration as 1.33 percent.

The statute gives the county one narrow break. With board of supervisors approval, the Treasurer may waive interest and penalties on a delinquency that occurs within a year after a mortgage or deed of trust on the property is satisfied or released. A taxpayer gets this waiver once per property. Ask the Treasurer whether your situation fits.

How big is the Pinal County housing market on paper?

Pinal County is among the fastest-growing counties in Arizona, and the Census Bureau figures show why bills and values move quickly here.

  • Population estimate for July 1, 2025: 539,380, up 26.6 percent from the April 2020 estimates base of 425,993.
  • Housing units estimated at 209,076, with 8,048 building permits issued in 2025.
  • Owner-occupied housing rate of 81.7 percent, with a median owner-occupied home value of $349,000 for 2020 to 2024.
  • Median household income of $80,266 and a mean commute of 31.8 minutes.

Those are county-wide medians from Census QuickFacts. A parcel in Apache Junction, Casa Grande, Maricopa or an unincorporated stretch near Florence can sit far from the median, so read your own Notice of Value rather than the county average.

How do I appeal my Pinal County valuation?

File a Petition for Review with the Pinal County Assessor within 60 days of the date the Notice of Valuation was mailed. The petition must state your opinion of full cash value and back it with a method: the income approach, the market approach with at least one comparable property or a sale of the property itself, or the cost approach. A postmark counts as the filing date, as ARS 42-16051 provides. The deadline for the 2026 value was April 15, 2025 and has passed, so watch for the next notice, which the Assessor must mail by March 1.

Use Form 82130R for a home and Form 82130 for commercial property, vacant land and agricultural land. The Assessor does not charge a fee, and you may ask for a meeting. The Assessor says it must use sales from the previous two years, so comparables from that window carry the most weight.

  • The Assessor must rule on petitions by August 15.
  • If the answer is a denial in whole or in part, you have 25 days to go to the County Board of Equalization. The county’s page sends these petitions to the Pinal County Board of Supervisors and says the State Board of Equalization hears them only for Maricopa and Pima counties.
  • The county board must decide, without exception, by October 15.
  • You may instead go to tax court within 60 days of the mailing of the last administrative decision, and the taxes must be paid before the delinquency date or the court dismisses the case.

Before you file, compare your full cash value with your limited property value. Taxes are computed on the limited value, which in most cases cannot rise more than 5 percent a year, and only the full cash value can be appealed. If the limited value is already below what you think the house is worth, winning the appeal will not cut this year’s tax. The details are on the county’s appeal page and appeal process page.

Which Pinal County property tax exemptions exist, and what happens when the owner sells?

The Assessor handles exemptions for widows, widowers and persons with a total and permanent disability under ARS 42-11111. Applications open the first Monday in January and close the last day of February. First-time applicants must apply in person. After that, renewals can be done by mail with a notary. The Assessor takes applications in Florence, Apache Junction, Casa Grande, Maricopa and San Tan Valley, and the number to call is 520-866-6361.

Income and net assessed value limits apply and they change every year, so take the current figures from the Assessor rather than a printed form. The widow and widower exemption now runs on a three-year cycle, while the disability exemption must be filed every year.

A sale ends the exemption on the sold house. The statute lists conveying title to another owner as a disqualifying event, and the property is taxed from that date. If you buy a new primary residence, you have 60 days to file an exemption transfer form with the county assessor where the new home sits. Exempt owners who are thinking about selling should call the Assessor before closing.

What happens to unpaid taxes in Pinal County?

The Treasurer sells delinquent taxes as liens at a tax lien sale held in February. The buyer pays your tax and holds a lien on the parcel, so what is sold is the lien and the house stays yours. The Treasurer also oversees deeding a parcel to the State of Arizona after five years of delinquent taxes.

Interest keeps running while a balance sits, and a lien on the parcel has to be cleared before you close. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure that includes prior years and interest through your closing date.

How do I handle a tax bill when I sell a house in Pinal County?

Get the full balance from the Treasurer before you list, and give that number to the title or escrow company handling the sale. Look up the parcel on the Treasurer’s site, then call to confirm whether any prior-year amounts, interest or a sold lien sit on top of the current bill.

  • Ask the Treasurer which half-year installments are paid and which are still open.
  • Ask the Assessor to confirm the mailing address on file so later bills reach the right person after closing.
  • If you hold a widow, widower or disability exemption, tell the Assessor the home is sold.

Assessor offices in the county are at 31 N Pinal Street, Building E in Florence; 575 N Idaho Road in Apache Junction; 820 E Cottonwood Lane in Casa Grande; 19955 N Wilson Avenue in Maricopa; and 31505 N Schnepf Road in San Tan Valley. Branch hours are shorter than the main office, so call before you drive.

When are Pinal County property taxes due?

The first half is due October 1 and the second half March 1. They go delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 1 and May 1. Bills of $100 or less are due October 1 and are delinquent after December 31. Paying the full year by December 31 avoids interest on the first half.

What interest does Pinal County charge on late property tax?

Sixteen percent a year, simple, from the delinquency date, with any part of a month counted as a full month. The Treasurer lists the proration as 1.33 percent a month. The Treasurer may waive interest once per property within a year after a mortgage or deed of trust is released, with board approval.

How long do I have to appeal my Pinal County property value?

You have 60 days from the date the Assessor mailed the Notice of Valuation, and a postmark counts. The Assessor must mail notices by March 1. The 2026 value deadline of April 15, 2025 has passed, so the next window opens with your next notice.

Can I appeal the limited property value in Pinal County?

No. State law allows an appeal only of full cash value or legal classification. The limited property value, which sets your tax, is calculated by a statutory formula and in most cases cannot rise more than 5 percent a year.

Does a widow or widower exemption carry over when the house is sold?

No. Conveying title to another owner ends the exemption on that property. You have 60 days after a new primary residence becomes your home to file an exemption transfer form with the assessor in the county where it sits.

Mohave County by the numbers

Which offices handle property tax in Mohave County, Arizona?

Two county offices split the work. The Mohave County Assessor sets the value and class of each parcel, and the Mohave County Treasurer sends the bill and collects the money. Both are in the county administration building at 700 West Beale Street in Kingman.

  • Assessor: (928) 753-0703, open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday, with field offices in Bullhead City (1130 Hancock Street) and Lake Havasu City (2001 College Drive, Suite 93), both closed noon to 1 p.m.
  • Treasurer: (928) 753-0737, open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday. Mail goes to PO Box 712, Kingman, AZ 86402.
  • Recorder: (928) 753-0701, which records the deed that changes the owner on the tax roll.

The Assessor's pamphlet says the office is not responsible for your tax rate. Cities, the county, school districts, fire districts and other districts each set their own, and your bill shows the share going to each. Mohave County has 258,932 parcels, so the Assessor and Treasurer both ask owners to quote the parcel number in every call or letter.

When are Mohave County property taxes due?

Tax bills go out by the first of October, and the first half is due October 1. For 2026, the Treasurer's site states that first-half payments became delinquent after November 2, which has already passed. The second half of the 2026 tax is due March 1, 2027.

November 1, 2026 fell on a Sunday, and the Treasurer's FAQ says a past-due date that lands on a weekend or holiday moves to 5:00 p.m. on the next business day. The same rule moves the second-half deadline: May 1, 2027 is a Saturday, so by that rule the cutoff would be Monday, May 3. The county honors postmarks on mailed payments.

Source: Mohave County Treasurer FAQ. Paying both halves in one payment by December 31 cancels the interest that began after November 1.

What is the penalty for late tax in Mohave County?

The penalty is 16% a year, prorated monthly starting on the first day of the month under A.R.S. 42-18053. The Treasurer states that this applies even if you never received a bill, because the law does not require the county to mail one.

Unpaid tax can end up at the annual tax lien sale. The 2026 Mohave County sale offered liens on parcels with 2024 delinquent taxes and any earlier years. A buyer of a lien pays a $10 non-refundable processing fee per certificate under A.R.S. 42-18116. Selling a lien does not hand over the house. It lets the lien buyer try to foreclose through Mohave County Superior Court once the statutory conditions are met.

Land with county-held liens older than five years can be deeded to the State and then offered at the March tax deed auction, held online. Winning bidders pay the bid plus 8.5% and a $40 processing fee. If your parcel is in that pipeline, the Treasurer at (928) 753-0737 can tell you what is owed and where the parcel stands.

How do you appeal a Mohave County valuation?

File a Petition for Review with the Assessor within 60 days of the postmark on the Notice of Value. Mohave County mails these notices no later than March 1 each year, and the clock starts at the notice, not at the tax bill.

The Arizona Department of Revenue form (82130R for residential) lays out the sequence. The Assessor must rule on appeals by August 15. If you disagree, you have 25 days after the decision was mailed to go to the County Board of Equalization, which must rule by October 15. After that, or in place of the administrative steps, you can file in Arizona Tax Court by December 15 of the valuation year, or within 60 days of the Board's mailed decision if that is later.

  • State the method behind your opinion of value. For the sales approach, give the price of at least one comparable property in the same area or the sale of your own parcel.
  • Only Full Cash Value and classification can be appealed. The Limited Property Value, which taxes are actually based on, follows a statutory formula.
  • Name an agent only with the Agency Authorization form attached.

The Assessor's pamphlet adds that the county holds BOE hearings in the Board of Supervisors auditorium in Kingman. The petition form is on the Assessor's forms page.

How does Mohave County calculate a tax bill?

The bill is Limited Property Value times the assessment ratio times the tax rate for your tax area. Limited value cannot rise more than 5% a year unless the property changes, such as a new pool or garage, and it cannot exceed Full Cash Value.

Class matters. The county's 2024 class table shows a primary residence at a 10% ratio, rental or leased residential at 10% in class 4.2, vacant land at 15% and commercial property at 16.5%, and the pamphlet warns that the Legislature changes ratios often. A house you rent out is taxed as class 4, and Arizona law requires an owner to register a residential rental with the Assessor. An owner who rents to a family member must register too.

Cities, the county and Mohave Community College are held to a 2% annual levy increase under Proposition 101, apart from new construction. School and fire districts are outside that cap. Mohave County is the same for every owner, but district taxes depend on where the parcel sits.

What tax relief exists for Mohave County homeowners?

The Assessor's office handles every exemption and valuation program, and the Treasurer's FAQ sends exemption questions there. The pamphlet lists the main ones.

  • Widow, widower and disability exemption: for Arizona residents under property value and income limits that the Assessor updates every year. Disability requires certification from a medical provider.
  • Veterans disability exemption: created by an Arizona ballot measure in 2022 and scaled to the VA disability rating. The Assessor's website carries a notice about a veteran exemption update for 2027.
  • Senior valuation protection: freezes the limited value of a primary residence for three years. At least one owner must be 65, the owner must have lived there at least two years, and applications run from January 2 through September 1. The freeze ends if the owner sells.
  • Tax deferral: for qualifying owners age 70 or older, filed with the Assessor between January 1 and March 31. Deferred tax plus interest becomes due when the property is transferred.
  • State Aid to Education: a reduction in the school portion of tax for owner-occupied homes.

How do you sell a Mohave County house when tax is due?

Start with a payoff figure. Ask the Treasurer for the amount owed on the parcel, including the monthly interest, and give it to the title company early so it can be cleared at closing.

The Treasurer's office will not accept online payment for prior years. Taxes for 2025 and earlier must be handled by calling (928) 753-0737, while 2026 tax can be paid online, by phone or in person. Checks go to the Mohave County Treasurer with the payment stub or parcel number, and the three drop boxes in Kingman, Bullhead City and Lake Havasu City take checks and money orders but never cash.

A seller who gets a bill after the sale can forward it to the buyer or mail it back to PO Box 712 with the date of sale and the buyer's name. A deferral or a valuation freeze also ends at sale, so tell the title company if you used either.

What kind of county is Mohave County for a home seller?

Mohave County covers 13,461 square miles in the northwest corner of Arizona, split in two by the Grand Canyon. The 2020 census counted 213,267 people, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 228,102.

Lake Havasu City, Bullhead City and Kingman are the three cities, with Kingman as county seat, and unincorporated communities such as Golden Valley, Fort Mohave, Mohave Valley and Dolan Springs lie outside city limits. Of the occupied homes counted in 2020, 71.7% were owner-occupied. For a parcel outside city limits, permits and zoning go through Mohave County Development Services at (928) 757-0903. Recording and ownership steps are covered in the Mohave County recorder guide.

More questions about Mohave County, AZ Property Tax Guide

When are property taxes due in Mohave County, AZ?

The first half is due October 1 and past due after 5:00 p.m. on November 1. The second half is due March 1 and past due after 5:00 p.m. on May 1. Taxes of $100 or less are due in full October 1 and past due after December 31.

What interest does Mohave County charge on late property tax?

The rate is 16% a year, prorated monthly from the first day of the month under A.R.S. 42-18053. The Treasurer applies it even when the owner never received a bill.

How long do I have to appeal my Mohave County property value?

You have 60 days from the postmark date of the Notice of Value, which the county mails no later than March 1. File a Petition for Review with the Assessor, then go to the County Board of Equalization within 25 days of the Assessor's decision if needed.

Can I pay prior-year Mohave County taxes online?

No. Only current-year taxes can be paid online. For 2025 and earlier years, call the Treasurer at (928) 753-0737. The Treasurer accepts mailed checks to PO Box 712, Kingman, AZ 86402.

Who do I contact about exemptions in Mohave County?

The Mohave County Assessor's Office at (928) 753-0703. The Assessor handles widow, widower, disability and veteran exemptions, the senior valuation protection option and rental registration.

Navajo County by the numbers

Who sends and collects property tax bills in Navajo County, Arizona?

The Navajo County Treasurer collects the tax, and the Navajo County Assessor sets values and handles exemptions and mailing addresses. The Treasurer's main office is at 100 East Code Talkers Drive in Holbrook, inside the county governmental center where State Routes 77 and 377 meet just south of town.

  • Treasurer, Holbrook: 928-524-4172, open Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Cash is accepted only at this office.
  • Treasurer, Show Low satellite: 600 North 9th Place, open Monday, Tuesday and Thursday 9:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m., Wednesday 9:00 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., closed Fridays.
  • Assessor: 928-524-4086.
  • Mail: Navajo County Treasurer, PO Box 668, Holbrook, AZ 86025-0668.

The Treasurer notes that all times are Arizona time and that Arizona does not observe daylight saving time, which matters if you are calling from out of state.

What is the Navajo County property tax calendar?

Navajo County mails one original bill each year, usually in mid to late September, and the first half is payable on October 1. For 2026 the first-half deadline of November 1 has passed. The next ones are the second half, payable March 1, 2027, and delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on May 1, 2027.

The county calendar says taxpayers are not penalized when the payment carries a postmark on or before the deadline date. Because November 1, 2026 fell on a Sunday and May 1, 2027 falls on a Saturday, ask the Treasurer how a weekend deadline is treated before you rely on the last day.

Source: Navajo County Property Tax Calendar.

What happens when Navajo County taxes go delinquent?

Interest starts at 16% a year, simple, charged monthly on the first of each month. The Treasurer's own arithmetic is 1.333% on the tax due, whether you pay on the first or the last day of the month. If the tax is still unpaid when the new year begins, an extra $5 or 5% penalty applies.

In February the lien for the unpaid tax is offered at an online auction. The Treasurer stresses that this is a sale of the lien for delinquent taxes, not a sale of your property. After three years from the sale date, the lien buyer can start foreclosure proceedings.

Once a lien has been sold, the Treasurer cannot accept partial payments to redeem it. The full amount of taxes, interest, penalties and fees is due, and the Treasurer requires certified funds, meaning cash, a cashier's check or a money order, for lien redemptions. Call 928-524-4172 for the exact payoff.

How do you challenge a Navajo County property valuation?

Petition the Assessor for review within 60 days of the notice date on the Notice of Valuation, or file directly with the tax court. The notice carries an appeal deadline date, and a postmark counts as the filing date.

  • The petition must state your opinion of full cash value and the method behind it. Market approach appeals need the sale price of at least one comparable property in the area or the sale of the property itself, and cost approach appeals need the cost to build plus the land value.
  • Limited Value is a statutory figure and cannot be appealed.
  • The Assessor must mail replies by August 15.
  • If you are still unhappy, the Board of Equalization appeal must be postmarked within 25 days of the Assessor's mailing date.
  • Without an administrative appeal, you have until December 15 of the year the notice was sent to go to Arizona Tax Court. With one, you have 60 days from the last decision, no later than December 15.

Personal property, which includes manufactured homes that were never affixed to the land, runs on a shorter clock: 20 days from the mailing of the valuation notice to petition the Assessor. The Treasurer cannot change a tax amount unless the Board of Supervisors directs it, so a wrong bill starts with the Assessor.

How is Navajo County tax figured, and who sets the rates?

Primary tax equals limited value times the assessment ratio times the primary rate, divided by $100. Secondary tax uses the same formula with the secondary rate, and the two add up to the total. Primary tax pays for operations, and secondary tax pays for special districts and voter-approved items such as bonds and budget overrides.

The Navajo County Board of Supervisors sets the county rate and the rates for the library district, public health service district, flood control district and the fire district assistance tax. Each city, town, school district and special district sets its own. Northland Pioneer College sets the rate for the community college. Fire District Assistance is a countywide levy under A.R.S. 48-807 that falls on every taxable property.

State Aid to Education cuts the school district's primary tax for owner-occupied primary residences and mobile homes, up to $600.

How are Navajo County taxes handled when you sell a house?

The title company prorates the year's tax on the settlement statement and credits the buyer for the seller's share. The Treasurer does not prorate between owners, and taxes are assessed against the property, not the person. Read the statement and ask the title company about any gap.

If the mortgage company paid your tax, it gets tax information from the Treasurer on request, and you can check payment history on the Property Information page under the Taxes tab. After closing, forward any bill to the new owner or mark it sold and return it.

To pay current-year tax by card or e-check, use the county's payment website or Point and Pay at 877-459-6499; a transaction fee applies and the county does not keep it. Payments can take 5 to 7 business days to appear online. For prior years, call 928-524-4172, and expect that the Treasurer may need to confirm amounts that the website does not show yet.

What is Navajo County like for property owners?

Navajo County covers 9,960 square miles of northern Arizona, and about 6,633 square miles are federal reservation land. The 2020 census counted 106,717 people, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 109,946. Holbrook is the seat, Show Low the largest city, and Winslow, Snowflake, Taylor, Pinetop-Lakeside and Kayenta make up the rest of the main towns.

The 2020 census counted 56,180 housing units, with 34.4% vacant, and 70.9% of occupied homes were owner-occupied. A bill for any parcel goes to the mailing address on file, so tell the Assessor at 928-524-4086 when that address changes, because tax notices are not forwarded. Deed steps are in the Navajo County recorder guide.

More questions about Navajo County, AZ Property Tax Guide

When are property taxes due in Navajo County, AZ?

Taxes can be paid in full by December 31, or in halves. The first half is due October 1 and delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1. The second half is due March 1 and delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on May 1.

What interest does Navajo County charge on delinquent taxes?

Interest is 16% a year, simple, prorated monthly, or 1.333% per month. A $5 or 5% penalty is added if the tax is not paid before January. Failure to receive a bill does not waive interest.

When is the Navajo County tax lien sale?

It is usually held online on the second Wednesday of February. A tax lien sale sells the lien on unpaid tax, not the property, and the buyer may begin foreclosure three years after the sale date.

How long do I have to appeal my Navajo County valuation?

You have 60 days from the notice date on the Notice of Valuation to petition the Assessor, or you can file directly with tax court. Board of Equalization appeals must be postmarked within 25 days of the Assessor's mailing date.

Does the Navajo County Treasurer prorate taxes when a house sells?

No. The title company prorates them at closing and gives the buyer credit for the seller's share. Taxes follow the property, so review the settlement statement.

Yavapai County by the numbers

Who handles property tax in Yavapai County?

Two county offices share the work. The Assessor sets the value of each parcel, and the Treasurer bills, collects and distributes the money to the county, Yavapai College, school districts, fire districts, special districts and cities. The Board of Supervisors adopts tax rates after the taxing districts submit their budgets and levies each August.

The Treasurer's Office has a counter in Prescott at 1015 Fair Street, 2nd floor, open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., phone (928) 771-3233. The Cottonwood Annex at 10 S 6th Street, phone (928) 639-8123, is open Monday through Thursday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., closed from noon to 1:00 p.m. and all day Friday. Email goes to web.treasurer@yavapaiaz.gov. The Assessor's number for valuation and exemption questions is (928) 771-3220.

Your bill carries a four-digit tax area code. Every parcel in the same code pays the same mix of jurisdictions, which always includes the county, the community college and one or more school districts, and may add a city, fire district or improvement district. Two houses a few miles apart can therefore carry different rates.

When are Yavapai County property taxes due?

Taxes come due in two halves. Under A.R.S. 42-18052, half is due October 1 and half the following March 1, and each half turns delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and May 1. When a delinquency date falls on a weekend or holiday, it moves to 5:00 p.m. on the next business day.

How do you pay a Yavapai County tax bill?

You can pay online, by phone, by mail or in person. The online and phone channels run through Certified Payments, and the fees go to that vendor, not to the Treasurer. Phone payments use 1-866-493-0416.

  • Electronic check: $0.40 per transaction, and one e-check can cover several parcels
  • Debit card: 1 percent of the amount, minimum $1.25
  • Credit card: 2.19 percent of the amount, minimum $1.25
  • Mail: Yavapai County Treasurer, 1015 Fair St., Prescott, AZ 86305, with the parcel number on the check
  • In person: the Prescott or Cottonwood counter

Allow three to five business days for mail and three business days for electronic payments to post. Pay the exact amount, because an overpayment is refunded. Owners who want paper bills replaced can register at eNoticesOnline with the authorization code on the front of the last bill. The Treasurer's page also links a 2027 tax bill estimator spreadsheet.

What happens if Yavapai County taxes go unpaid?

Unpaid tax grows at 16 percent simple interest per year from the time of delinquency, and a fraction of a month counts as a whole month, according to A.R.S. 42-18053. Interest is not collected if the full year is paid by December 31 of the tax year or if the delinquency came from an assessor or treasurer error. The treasurer may waive interest once per property for a delinquency within one year after a mortgage or deed of trust is released, with Board of Supervisors approval.

The tax is also a lien. A.R.S. 42-17153 says it attaches on January 1 of the tax year and takes priority over other liens and encumbrances, apart from state liens and liens for taxes of other years. Yavapai County runs an annual online tax lien auction. The last one was February 10, 2026, and the next is set for February 9, 2027. Properties deeded to the state for back taxes are offered separately on the Board of Supervisors' Tax Deed Sales page.

How do you appeal a Yavapai County valuation?

File a Petition for Review with the Assessor by the date printed on your Notice of Value, which is mailed by March 1. The Assessor's Value Notices page puts that window at 60 days from the postmark. Petition forms are available from the Assessor's website during the filing period or at either Assessor office, and the forms come with instructions.

  • Notice of Change: mailed by September 30 for new construction, additions, splits or changes in use. File with the County Board of Equalization within 25 days of the mailing date. A state-certified hearing officer hears the appeal.
  • Tax Court: if you disagree with the Assessor or the Board, file within 60 days of the Board's decision or by December 15, whichever is later.
  • Skip the administrative step: you may file directly in Tax Court, but no later than December 15 of the valuation year.
  • Buyers: if you bought before December 15 of the valuation year, you may appeal to Tax Court by that date. After that date, the new owner has until December 15 of the year the taxes are levied.

The county says the Full Cash Value is the appealable figure. Taxes are computed from the Limited Property Value, which can rise only 5 percent a year unless the property changed, and the Assessor reports that 95 percent of Yavapai parcels fall in that category.

Which exemptions and relief programs can lower the bill?

The Assessor takes applications for personal exemptions in person, Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., at either office. The season runs from the first Monday in January through the last business day of February. Exemptions cover widows and widowers, totally and permanently disabled persons, disabled veterans and surviving spouses of disabled veterans.

Veteran rules are changing. A veteran with a 100 percent service-connected disability, or total disability based on individual unemployability, gets a full exemption on the primary residence starting with tax year 2026, with income limits still applying that year. Legislation passed in 2026 removes the income limit beginning with tax year 2027. Other qualifying veterans receive the annual exemption amount the state sets. The Assessor's calendar also lists September 1 as the last day to apply for the Senior Freeze program.

Owner-occupied homes already receive a State Aid reduction on the primary school district tax, shown on the bill, and the state reimburses the school districts. Ask the Assessor at (928) 771-3220 which documents to bring, including an Arizona driver's license and a VA award letter for veteran claims.

What do you owe on a Yavapai County home you are selling?

Ask the Treasurer for the amount due on the parcel before you list, then settle it at closing through escrow. The county's tax inquiry website lets you search by parcel number and view a bill, and the Treasurer's FAQ says taxes due are the responsibility of the current owner. If the bill lands after the sale, the new owner or the mortgage company pays that year's bill.

Timing matters in this county. The Assessor's November 2, 2026 release puts the 2026 median single-family price at $539,000 through October, down from $555,000 in 2025. A seller with delinquent years should also remember that interest runs at 16 percent and the lien sale happens each February.

Yavapai County stretches across 8,128 square miles, with Prescott as the county seat, so a house in Chino Valley, Camp Verde or Sedona can sit in a different tax area from one in Prescott Valley. Check the code on your bill.

More questions about Yavapai County, AZ Property Tax Guide

When is the second half of Yavapai County property tax due?

The second half is due March 1 and becomes delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on May 1 under A.R.S. 42-18052. Because May 1, 2027 is a Saturday, the delinquency moves to 5:00 p.m. on Monday, May 3, 2027. You can also pay the full year by December 31 with no charged interest.

How much interest does Yavapai County charge on late property tax?

Delinquent taxes bear 16 percent simple interest per year, and a part of a month counts as a full month under A.R.S. 42-18053. There is no interest if the full year is paid by December 31 of the tax year or if an assessor or treasurer error caused the delinquency.

How long do I have to appeal my Yavapai County property value?

You have 60 days from the postmark on the Notice of Value, which is mailed by March 1. For a Notice of Change, mailed by September 30, you have 25 days from the mailing date to go to the County Board of Equalization. Tax Court filings generally close on December 15.

Who pays property tax when a Yavapai County house sells?

The current owner is responsible for taxes due, according to the Treasurer's FAQ, and escrow normally settles the open amount at closing. If a bill arrives after the sale, the new owner or the mortgage company pays the current year's bill. Ask the Treasurer for the parcel's balance first.

Can I pay Yavapai County property tax by credit card?

Yes. Certified Payments charges 2.19 percent with a $1.25 minimum for credit cards, 1 percent with a $1.25 minimum for debit cards, and $0.40 for an electronic check. The fee goes to the vendor, not the Treasurer. Pay online from the Treasurer's page or call 1-866-493-0416.

Coconino County by the numbers

How large is Coconino County and what does it include?

Coconino County covers 18,661 square miles in north-central Arizona, which makes it the largest county in the state and the second largest in the contiguous United States after San Bernardino County, California. It has more land than nine U.S. states.

Flagstaff is the county seat and the largest city. The county was created in 1891 after residents of the northern part of Yavapai County, tired of traveling to Prescott for county business, petitioned for their own jurisdiction. It takes in Grand Canyon National Park, the Flagstaff metropolitan area, and parts of the Navajo, Hualapai, Hopi, Havasupai and Kaibab reservations, which together account for 7,142 square miles.

One office pair, the Coconino County Assessor and Treasurer, handles property valuation and tax collection across all of it.

What does Coconino County look like in Census numbers?

The 2020 census counted 145,101 people in Coconino County, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 144,368. The housing count stands out because a quarter of the units were vacant.

With about 41 percent of occupied homes rented and a median age of 32.5, Coconino County has a younger, more renter-heavy mix than many Arizona counties, and a quarter of its housing units were vacant on census day. A landlord in Flagstaff or Page selling a rental will want the tax balance, the tenant file and any repair list in hand before a closing.

What drives the Coconino County economy?

Education, health care, a manufacturer, and tourism sit at the top. A 2017 list of the county's largest employers put Northern Arizona University first at 3,500 workers, followed by W. L. Gore and Associates at 3,060 and Flagstaff Medical Center at 2,180, with the Flagstaff Unified School District at 1,590 and Aramark at 1,310.

The Bureau of Economic Analysis counted 87,159 jobs in the county in 2019. Accommodation and food services was the biggest sector at 14,472 jobs, or 16.6 percent, roughly double the national share of 7.5 percent. Health care and social assistance came next at 9,901 jobs, and state government held 8,078, about triple the national share.

For a seller, that mix means house demand and rental demand can follow the university calendar and the visitor season. If a house has been used as a short-term rental, ask the city or county whether any license carries over to a new owner.

How do you get around Coconino County, and why does it matter for a sale?

Flagstaff is a highway junction where Interstate 40 runs east and west and Interstate 17 runs south to Phoenix. U.S. 89 and 180 lead north toward the Grand Canyon.

  • Flagstaff Pulliam Airport, four miles south of downtown, is served by two commercial airlines.
  • Grand Canyon National Park Airport is in Tusayan.
  • Amtrak's Southwest Chief stops in Flagstaff.
  • The Mountain Line runs buses around Flagstaff.
  • The Grand Canyon Railway links Williams with the South Rim.

An owner living in another state can get to Flagstaff by air, which helps with signing and walk-throughs. Parts of the county are reservation land, so ask a title company early about any parcel that might sit on or near it.

Which Coconino County communities and school districts might a seller deal with?

Flagstaff had 65,870 people in the 2010 census, ahead of Sedona at 10,031, Tuba City at 8,611, Page at 7,247 and Williams at 3,023. Fredonia and Tusayan are the county's two incorporated towns.

Sedona sits mostly in Yavapai County, so confirm which county bills a Sedona address before you call an office. The county's K-12 districts are Ash Fork, Flagstaff, Fredonia-Moccasin, Grand Canyon, Page, Sedona-Oak Creek, Tuba City and Williams, plus the Chevelon Butte and Maine Consolidated elementary districts. Two charter schools, Flagstaff Arts and Leadership Academy and Northland Preparatory Academy, also operate here.

Higher education includes Northern Arizona University, Coconino County Community College and a Diné College center in Tuba City.

When do Coconino County property tax payments come due?

Half of the year's tax is due October 1 and half on March 1, and unpaid halves become delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and May 1, respectively, under A.R.S. 42-18052. Bills of $100 or less are due in one piece on October 1 and delinquent after December 31 at 5:00 p.m.

The Coconino County Treasurer's office is at 110 E. Cherry Avenue in Flagstaff and keeps hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday. Contact options published on its tax portal:

  • Phone: (928) 679-8188 or (877) 500-1818.
  • Email: treasurer@coconino.az.gov.
  • Automated payment line: 877-884-8060, where you give your tax account or parcel number.
  • Online: enter an account or parcel number in the Treasurer's portal, choose the first half, second half or full payment link, and finish at a third-party payment page.

What does it cost to pay late in Coconino County?

Unpaid tax carries 16 percent simple interest per year after it turns delinquent, with partial months rounded up to whole months (A.R.S. 42-18053). Paying the full year's tax by December 31 of the tax year stops the interest, and interest is not collected where the county's own error caused the delinquency.

An owner who has just paid off a mortgage and then falls behind on taxes can ask for a one-time interest waiver, which needs the county board of supervisors' approval.

How does the lien work if you sell a Coconino County house?

Property tax is a lien on the property that attaches on January 1 of the tax year, and it ranks ahead of nearly all other liens (A.R.S. 42-17153). It stays until the tax is paid in full, until a tax sale purchaser takes title, or until a certificate of removal and abatement issues.

When a Coconino County owner signs a contract, the escrow officer asks the Treasurer for the balance. The amount due, with interest if any, is deducted from the seller's proceeds. A payoff is a standard line on a settlement statement.

How do you challenge a Coconino County valuation?

Start with the assessor's annual notice of value, which Arizona law requires to be mailed before March 1 (A.R.S. 42-15101). Then file a petition for review within 60 days of the mailing date, counting the postmark as the filing date (A.R.S. 42-16051).

The petition needs the owner's opinion of the full cash value and a stated method, such as at least one comparable property or the recent sale of the home. The assessor can amend a notice within 60 days of mailing if a data error affected a group of properties, and after that the roll can change only through the appeal process.

Confirm your own dates with the Assessor's Office, since the notice date can differ by year.

More questions about Coconino County, AZ Property Tax Guide

Where do I pay Coconino County property tax?

You can pay online through the Treasurer's portal, by calling the automated line at 877-884-8060, or at the Treasurer's office at 110 E. Cherry Avenue in Flagstaff. Have your account number or parcel number ready.

What are the Coconino County Treasurer's hours?

The Treasurer's tax portal lists hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday. Call (928) 679-8188 or (877) 500-1818 to confirm before you visit.

How much interest applies to late Coconino County taxes?

Delinquent taxes bear 16 percent simple interest per year under Arizona law. Interest is waived if the full year is paid by December 31 or the delinquency was caused by a county error.

Is Coconino County the largest county in Arizona?

Yes. At 18,661 square miles, Coconino County is the largest county in Arizona and the second largest in the contiguous United States.

Can I sell a Coconino County house if the tax bill is unpaid?

Yes. The bill is a lien that has to be paid at closing, and the amount comes out of the seller's proceeds. The title company will get the balance from the Treasurer.

Yuma County by the numbers

Which Yuma County offices handle property tax?

Two offices split the work. The Yuma County Assessor values and classifies every parcel, and the Yuma County Treasurer sends the bills and collects the money. Both sit at 197 S. Main Street in Yuma, AZ 85364, with the Treasurer in Suite 203.

  • Assessor: 928-373-6040 or assr-info@yumacountyaz.gov. Questions about value, land use classification, exemptions and petitions go here.
  • Treasurer: 928-539-7781 or treasury@yumacountyaz.gov. Statements, payments, delinquent accounts and the February tax lien sale go here.
  • Board of Supervisors: 928-373-1010. The Board acts as the board of equalization for appeals and keeps the list of state tax-deeded parcels.

The Assessor has no control over tax rates or levies. Those come from school districts, cities, fire districts and the county, so a complaint about the size of a bill belongs at their budget hearings.

What should a home seller know about Yuma County itself?

Yuma County fills the southwest corner of Arizona, a county of 5,519 square miles that borders Imperial County, California across the Colorado River and shares a line with Mexico to the south. It was one of Arizona's four original counties, created by the first Territorial Legislature in 1864. The seat started at La Paz, moved in 1871 to Arizona City, and took the name Yuma in 1873.

The Census Bureau counted 203,881 residents in 2020 and estimated 224,449 for July 2025. Yuma is the county seat and largest city, joined by the cities of San Luis and Somerton and the town of Wellton.

Farming drives much of the economy. Yuma County leads Arizona in crop sales by dollar value, and the winter vegetable season from November to March supplies a large share of the country's leafy greens. Census figures for 2020 to 2024 put the median value of an owner-occupied home at $217,800, the owner-occupied rate at 71.0 percent and median household income at $62,876.

When are Yuma County property taxes due?

Taxes come due in two halves: the first on October 1 and the second on March 1. Each half turns delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on the next November 1 and May 1, and a weekend or legal holiday pushes that cutoff to the next business day. For 2026 the first-half deadline was 5:00 p.m. on Monday, November 2, so it has already passed.

  • A bill of $100 or less is due in full on October 1 and turns delinquent after December 31.
  • Interest runs at 16 percent a year, simple, and any part of a month counts as a full month.
  • No interest is charged when the delinquency traces to an Assessor or Treasurer error, or when the full year is paid by December 31 of the tax year.
  • The Treasurer's calendar adds a 5 percent penalty on taxes still delinquent on January 1.
  • With Board of Supervisors approval, the Treasurer may waive interest and penalties once per property for a delinquency that falls within a year after a mortgage is paid off.

Missing a statement does not excuse a late payment. The Treasurer advises anyone who pays their own taxes and has no statement by October 15 to call the office or use the online portal at yumacountyaz.gov/paytaxes.

How does the tax lien affect a sale in Yuma County?

The lien for a year's tax attaches on January 1 of that tax year, and it ranks ahead of every other lien on the parcel except liens held by the state and liens for taxes from other years (A.R.S. 42-17153). That means an unpaid bill travels with the house into escrow. Ask your closing agent to request a payoff figure from the Treasurer before the closing date.

If a lender pays your taxes through an impound account, confirm with the servicer that the county actually received the payment. New owners should also confirm their name and mailing address with the Assessor before bills go out.

Classification matters to the next owner. A parcel coded 3.01 is an owner-occupied primary residence and already gets the Less State to Education reduction from the Treasurer, while code 4.02 marks rental use. To change a code, the buyer files an Affidavit of Primary Residence with the Assessor along with proof such as an Arizona driver's license, ID card, voter registration card or state income tax return. The office will not change the class until it has one of those documents.

How do you appeal a Yuma County property valuation?

You file a Petition for Review with the Assessor within 60 days after the notice of value was mailed (A.R.S. 42-16051), and the deadline is printed on your notice. The 2027 notices went out on February 20, 2026, with an appeal date of April 20, 2026, so that window has closed. Notices for the following year are due by March 1.

  • Step one: the Assessor reviews the petition and may inspect the property. You can then ask for a meeting with the Assessor or a representative.
  • Step two: if you still disagree, appeal to the Board of Equalization, which in Yuma County is the Board of Supervisors. The filing is due within 25 days after the Assessor's decision is mailed (A.R.S. 42-16056), and you cannot raise an issue that was missing from the original petition.
  • Step three: tax court or superior court. The county calendar lists December 15 as the last day to file a tax court appeal. Small claims procedures are open when a residence is valued under $300,000 or the tax bill is under $5,000.

The Assessor accepts four grounds: wrong facts on the property record such as square footage, a full cash value out of line with recent neighborhood sales, an income approach that shows the value is excessive, or a limited property value calculated incorrectly. Arguing that your taxes are too high does not qualify.

Which tax relief programs apply to Yuma County homeowners?

Arizona offers several exemptions and a valuation freeze, and the Assessor processes all of them. The dollar limits adjust every year, so ask the office for the current figures before you rely on any number.

  • Widow, widower and total and permanent disability exemption: file with the Assessor between the first working day of January and March 1. The claimant must stay under the statutory income limit and renew eligibility each year (A.R.S. 42-11111).
  • Veterans: a primary residence owned by a veteran with a 100 percent service-connected rating is fully exempt, and smaller ratings earn a partial exemption. A further veterans exemption under House Bill 4168 takes effect for tax year 2027, and applications open January 4, 2027, according to the Assessor.
  • Senior Property Valuation Protection Option, often called the senior freeze: filing period runs from January 1 to September 1.

Selling changes the picture. Under A.R.S. 42-11111, conveying title to another owner is a disqualifying event, and a person who moves must file an exemption transfer form with the assessor of the county where the new primary residence sits within 60 days of moving in.

What happens to unpaid taxes in Yuma County?

Parcels that still owe prior-year tax at the end of December become candidates for the Treasurer's tax lien sale the following February. For the 2025 tax year the sale is set for February 18, 2027, and owners can stop it by paying in full by 5:00 p.m. the day before.

An investor who buys the lien takes over the right to collect the debt, and the state's lien statutes also let the Treasurer foreclose the right to redeem (A.R.S. 42-18101). Do not confuse this sale with the Board of Supervisors' sale of real property held by the state under a tax deed. That list is prepared on or before the first Monday in November, and the Board can be reached at 928-373-1010.

December 31 is the cutoff for interest-free full-year payment and January 1 brings the 5 percent penalty, so a seller with an old balance gains the most by paying before the year turns.

What should you check before listing a Yuma County house?

  • Search your parcel on the Treasurer's payment portal and note whether both 2026 halves show as paid.
  • Check the class code on your notice of value.
  • If you hold a widow, disability, veteran or senior freeze benefit, ask the Assessor how it ends at sale and how to transfer it.
  • Have your closing agent order a payoff statement from the Treasurer once an offer is accepted.

More questions about Yuma County, AZ Property Tax Guide

Has the 2026 first-half deadline in Yuma County passed?

Yes. The first half was due October 1 and turned delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 2, 2026. The Treasurer says that paying both installments by December 31 avoids interest on the first half, so a balance can still be cleared before year end.

Can I sell a Yuma County house with unpaid property tax?

The tax lien stays attached to the parcel, so the amount owed has to be paid or accounted for at closing. Ask your closing agent to request a payoff figure from the Treasurer at 928-539-7781 so the interest through the closing date is included.

What interest rate does Yuma County charge on late taxes?

The rate is 16 percent a year, simple interest, counted by the month with any fraction treated as a full month. Interest is waived when the delinquency comes from a county error or when the whole year is paid by December 31 of the tax year.

How long do I have to appeal my Yuma County valuation?

You have 60 days from the mailing date of the notice of value to petition the Assessor, and the exact date is printed on the notice. If the Assessor denies the request, you have 25 days after the decision is mailed to appeal to the Board of Equalization.

Does selling my home end my Arizona property tax exemption?

Yes. Conveying title to another owner is a disqualifying event under A.R.S. 42-11111. If you buy a new primary residence, you must file an exemption transfer form with the county assessor within 60 days after it becomes your primary residence.

Cochise County by the numbers

Where is Cochise County and how big is it?

Cochise County fills the southeastern corner of Arizona and borders both New Mexico and the Mexican state of Sonora. It covers 6,219 square miles, about the size of Rhode Island and Connecticut put together, so a seller here may be dealing with a town house in Sierra Vista or a few acres an hour's drive from the nearest stoplight.

The county was carved out of eastern Pima County on February 1, 1881. Tombstone was the first county seat, and the seat moved to Bisbee in 1929, where the art deco courthouse still stands.

Property tax bills for every parcel in the county run through the same two offices, the County Assessor for value and the County Treasurer for collection. The rules they follow come from Arizona statute, which we summarize below with links to the text.

What do the Census numbers say about housing in Cochise County?

The 2020 census counted 125,447 residents and 58,648 housing units in Cochise County, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 126,332 people. Most occupied homes are owned by the people living in them.

A median age of 44 and nearly a quarter of residents past 65 mean that a fair share of Cochise County houses change hands after a death or a move to be near family. Those sales often come with a property tax bill that nobody has opened in months.

Which Cochise County towns matter most to a house seller?

Sierra Vista is the largest city, and Douglas, Bisbee, Benson, Willcox and Tombstone are the other incorporated cities, with Huachuca City as the lone incorporated town. The 2010 census counts show how uneven the county is.

  • Sierra Vista: 43,888 people, plus another 14,797 in the Sierra Vista Southeast area just outside the city.
  • Douglas: 17,378 people, on the Mexican border.
  • Bisbee: 5,575 people, the county seat.
  • Benson: 5,105 people, on Interstate 10.
  • Willcox: 3,757 people.
  • Tombstone: 1,380 people.

Many Cochise County homes sit outside any city, in unincorporated communities such as Whetstone, St. David, Elfrida and Palominas. Rural parcels outside city limits can differ a lot from a town lot, so ask the Assessor and the title company what applies to yours.

How do Fort Huachuca and the border shape the local housing market?

Fort Huachuca, the Army installation inside Sierra Vista, gives that city a heavy military presence, and Douglas, Naco and Agua Prieta sit on the Mexican line. Owners near the post may be selling on a timeline set by a move rather than by the market.

Getting to the county is a matter of roads. Interstate 10 crosses it, and the state routes include 80, 82, 83, 90, 92, 181 and 186, along with U.S. 191. Cochise County has no commercial flights, and the nearest commercial airport is in Tucson, about 70 miles from Sierra Vista. Sellers who live out of state should plan trips with that drive in mind, because signing, inspections and key handoffs often happen in person.

Visitors come for Chiricahua National Park, Kartchner Caverns State Park, Coronado National Memorial and the San Pedro Riparian National Conservation Area, among other protected places. Homes near these sites are a different kind of listing from a tract house in Sierra Vista.

When are Cochise County property taxes due?

Arizona law splits a year's real property tax into two halves, due October 1 and the following March 1. The first half turns delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 1, and the second half after 5:00 p.m. on May 1 (A.R.S. 42-18052).

InstallmentDueDelinquent after
First halfOctober 15:00 p.m. on November 1
Second halfMarch 15:00 p.m. on May 1
Total bill of $100 or lessOctober 1, all at once5:00 p.m. on December 31

If a delinquency date lands on a weekend or legal holiday, the deadline moves to 5:00 p.m. on the next business day. The statute is short and worth reading once.

How much interest does an unpaid Cochise County tax bill earn?

Delinquent taxes accrue interest at 16 percent a year, simple, counted from the delinquency date, and any part of a month counts as a full month (A.R.S. 42-18053). That makes a missed first half more expensive every month the house sits.

The same statute lists situations where interest is not collected:

  • The delinquency came from a mistake by the county assessor or treasurer.
  • The full year's tax is paid on or before December 31 of the tax year, even if the first half was late.
  • The treasurer waives interest, with board of supervisors approval, for a delinquency in the year after a mortgage or deed of trust on the property was released. A taxpayer gets this waiver once per property.

For a seller, the December 31 rule is the practical one. If the first half slipped past November 1, paying the whole year before year end can erase the interest, so it is worth doing before a closing rather than leaving it to a payoff statement.

Read the full interest statute before relying on any waiver.

Does a tax lien affect selling a Cochise County house?

Yes. A property tax is a lien on the assessed property, it attaches on January 1 of the tax year, and it outranks nearly every other lien except those held by the state and liens for taxes of other years (A.R.S. 42-17153).

The lien stays until the taxes, penalties, charges and interest are paid, until title vests in a purchaser at a tax sale, or until a certificate of removal and abatement is issued. A buyer's title company will therefore ask the Treasurer for the amount owed and require payment at or before closing.

This matters most for two kinds of Cochise County owners. One is the heir of a house where the last owner stopped paying. The other is a landlord who let a bill ride while a tenant left. In both cases the lien stays with the property, and a payoff is normally taken from the sale proceeds at closing.

How does the Cochise County Assessor's notice of value work?

The assessor must mail every owner of record a notice of full cash value and, where it applies, limited property value, on a date before March 1 each year (A.R.S. 42-15101). The notice also goes to a purchaser under a deed of trust or an agreement of sale.

If an owner thinks the number is wrong, a petition to the assessor is the first step. It must be filed within 60 days after the notice was mailed, and a postmark counts as the filing date (A.R.S. 42-16051). The petition has to give the owner's opinion of value and the method behind it. Under the market approach, that means at least one comparable property or the sale of the property itself.

If an owner died and the house passed by beneficiary deed, the notice goes to the dead owner's old address until the beneficiary sends the assessor a written notice with a certified death certificate and a new address. Families who inherit a Cochise County house this way should send that letter early, because a missed notice means a missed 60-day window.

Which Cochise County school districts might appear on a parcel?

Ten unified districts serve the county: Benson, Bisbee, Bowie, Douglas, Fort Huachuca Accommodation, San Simon, St. David, Sierra Vista, Tombstone and Willcox. Valley Union is a high school district, and eleven small elementary districts, such as Apache, Ash Creek, Cochise, Double Adobe, Elfrida, McNeal, Naco, Palominas, Pearce, Pomerene and Rucker, cover other areas.

The district a parcel falls into is a fact to confirm with the County Assessor.

More questions about Cochise County, AZ Property Tax Guide

When is the second half of Cochise County property tax due?

The second half is due March 1 and becomes delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on May 1, under Arizona's statute on due dates. If May 1 falls on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day.

What interest rate applies to late Cochise County property tax?

Delinquent taxes carry 16 percent simple interest per year, with a partial month counted as a full month. Interest is not collected if the full year's tax is paid by December 31 of the tax year.

Can I sell a Cochise County house with unpaid property taxes?

Yes, you can. The unpaid tax is a lien that must be satisfied at closing, so the payoff comes out of the sale proceeds. A title company will request the exact amount from the Treasurer.

How long do I have to appeal my Cochise County valuation?

You have 60 days after the assessor mailed the notice of value to file a petition with the assessor. A postmark date counts as the filing date.

Does Cochise County have an airport with commercial flights?

No commercial flights serve the county, according to the Wikipedia county article. The nearest commercial airport is in Tucson, about 70 miles from Sierra Vista.
