Gila County by the numbers

Who bills and collects property tax in Gila County, Arizona?

The Gila County Treasurer bills and collects the tax, and the Gila County Assessor sets the values the bills are built on. The Treasurer's office collects real and personal property tax for the county and for the school, fire, sanitary, water, flood control and improvement districts and the city and town governments inside it.

Gila County covers 4,795 square miles. Globe is the county seat and Payson is the largest town, and both host county offices. Contacts:

  • Treasurer, Globe: 1400 E. Ash, Globe, AZ 85501, phone 928-402-8702 or 928-402-8703.

Questions about the size of a rate go to the district that set it. The Treasurer's page also offers online payment.

When are Gila County property taxes due?

Half of the bill is due October 1 and the other half March 1. Each half goes delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on the following November 1 and May 1. A.R.S. 42-18052 adds that when the delinquency date lands on a weekend or legal holiday, the cutoff moves to 5:00 p.m. on the next business day.

That rule matters this year. November 1, 2026 fell on a Sunday, so the first half of the 2026 bill became delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on Monday, November 2, 2026. That date has passed, and interest is running on any unpaid first half. The second half is due Monday, March 1, 2027. May 1, 2027 is a Saturday, so the second half goes delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on Monday, May 3, 2027.

What does paying late cost in Gila County?

Late taxes carry 16 percent simple interest per year, and part of a month counts as a whole month under A.R.S. 42-18053. The Treasurer's tax notice describes the same charge as one and one third percent per month, stepping up on the first day of each month.

Interest is not charged in a few situations:

  • You pay the full year's tax on or before December 31 of the tax year.
  • The delinquency came from an error by the county assessor or the county treasurer.

Not receiving a statement does not remove the debt. A.R.S. 42-18054 says liability for the tax and any interest does not depend on the owner or the lender receiving the statement. The county mails one original bill per year, so if a lender pays your taxes, confirm that the lender requested the bill.

How does Gila County value and tax a house?

The Assessor mails a Notice of Value on or before March 1 each year, and the tax is figured on the Limited Property Value, not the market figure. Every property carries both a Full Cash Value, which is the market-based number, and a Limited Property Value. The limited value can rise no more than 5 percent a year unless the property changes, for example through an addition or a parcel split.

The notice also shows a legal class that sets the assessment ratio:

  • Class 3, owner or qualified family member's primary residence: 10 percent.
  • Class 4.1, owner's non-primary residence: 10 percent.
  • Class 4.2, residential rental: 10 percent.
  • Class 2, vacant land and other property: 15 percent.
  • Class 1, commercial and industrial: 16 percent.

The county notes these ratios can change yearly. Rates come last. Under A.R.S. 42-17151 each county, city, school and community college governing body sets its levy on or before the third Monday in August, and the tax statements go out in late September or early October.

How do you appeal a Gila County valuation?

File a Petition for Review with the Assessor within 60 days of the date the Notice of Value was mailed. A.R.S. 42-16051 sets that window and requires you to state your opinion of full cash value with supporting information, such as a comparable property or the sale of your own home.

The county offers three forms: Form 82130R for residential property, Form 82130 for vacant land and commercial property, and Form 82131 for multiple parcels. Mail or email the completed form to Gila County Assessor's Office, ATTN: Appeals, 1400 E Ash Street, Globe, AZ 85501. The county rejects appeals filed on the wrong or an incomplete form.

  • The Assessor must send its decision before August 15 of the valuation year.
  • To continue, file with the County Board of Equalization within 25 days of the date the Assessor sent the decision. You cannot go to the Board without first appealing to the Assessor.
  • Arizona Tax Court is the next step after the Board, within 60 days of the date the hearing officer's decision is mailed.
  • If you missed the 60-day window, the county says you can still appeal to Tax Court before December 15 of the valuation year.

The next Notices of Value arrive before March 1, 2027.

Which Gila County property tax relief programs exist?

The Assessor runs the widow, widower, disability and veteran exemptions and the Senior Freeze. None is automatic, and the county encourages people to apply even if they doubt they qualify.

For tax year 2026 the exemption is worth up to $4,873 of assessed value for widows, widowers and people with a total and permanent disability. Two limits apply: all property you own in Arizona cannot exceed $36,454 of assessed limited value, and household income from 2025 cannot exceed $39,865 with no children under 18 or $47,826 with children. A disabled veteran with a 100 percent VA rating has no cap on the primary residence and no property value limit. Applications run from January 2 to March 1, and first-time applicants apply in person at the Globe or Payson office.

The Senior Freeze holds the Limited Property Value of a primary residence for three years. The owner must be at least 65, must have lived in the home for two years, and must stay under a three-year average income of $47,712 for one owner or $59,640 for two or more owners. Applications run January 2 through September 1. The freeze ends if the owner sells or rents. Taxes themselves are not frozen.

What happens to unpaid property tax in Gila County?

Unpaid taxes become a tax lien that the Treasurer offers for sale each February. A.R.S. 42-18101 directs the Treasurer to sell the liens and to foreclose the right to redeem. Gila County runs its sale online, and the list of parcels is published in the Silver Belt and Payson Roundup.

A buyer of the lien pays the delinquent amount and then pays the later years' taxes each June until the owner redeems or the lien is foreclosed. The Treasurer's office also oversees deeding property to the State of Arizona when parcels have five years of delinquent taxes.

What should a Gila County seller do about property tax before closing?

Ask the Treasurer for the amount due on your parcel, including any interest through your expected closing date. Then ask your title or escrow company how this year's bill will be divided between you and the buyer.

  • Look up the parcel through the Treasurer's online tax bill search by name, account number or parcel number.
  • Check whether the first half of the current bill has been paid. For 2026 the first half went delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 2.

What is Gila County like for people selling a house?

Gila County sits in the central part of the state, and Globe began as a mining community. The county was formed from parts of Maricopa and Pinal counties on February 8, 1881, and it includes parts of the Fort Apache and San Carlos Indian Reservations. The incorporated places are Globe, Payson, Miami, Hayden, Star Valley and Winkelman. Schools are run by the Globe, Hayden-Winkelman, Miami, Payson, San Carlos and Whiteriver unified school districts.

The Census Bureau puts the 2025 population at 53,801 and counts 33,259 housing units. The median value of an owner-occupied home was $269,400 for 2020 through 2024, owners live in 77.5 percent of occupied homes, and median household income was $61,986. In the 2020 census, 31.1 percent of housing units were vacant.

More questions about Gila County, AZ Property Tax Guide

When is the second half of Gila County property tax due?

The second half is due March 1 and becomes delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on May 1. For the 2026 tax year that means due Monday, March 1, 2027, and delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on Monday, May 3, 2027, because May 1 is a Saturday.

Can I pay my whole Gila County bill at once?

Yes. Paying the full year's tax on or before December 31 of the tax year avoids interest under A.R.S. 42-18053. For 2026 that is Thursday, December 31.

What if I missed the 60-day window to appeal my Gila County valuation?

You can still file in Arizona Tax Court before December 15 of the valuation year, according to the Gila County Assessor. Tax Court filings go through the Maricopa County Superior Court, so do not send those forms to the Assessor.

Who qualifies for the Senior Freeze in Gila County?

An owner who is at least 65, has lived in the primary residence for two years, and has a three-year average income under $47,712 for one owner or $59,640 for two or more owners. Applications are accepted January 2 through September 1, and renewal is needed every three years.

Where do I pay Gila County property tax?

You can pay online through the Treasurer's payment portal, in person at 1400 E. Ash in Globe, in Payson at 707 S. Colcord Rd. on Tuesdays and Thursdays, or by mail to P.O. Box 1093, Globe, AZ 85502. The Treasurer's direct line is 928-402-8702 or 928-402-8703.

Which Apache County offices deal with property tax?

Three offices in St. Johns split the work: the Assessor values property, the Treasurer bills and collects, and the Recorder holds the deed records. All three list 75 West Cleveland as their address and keep Monday to Thursday hours, 6:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., closed Friday.

The Treasurer sends tax revenue to the taxing districts, such as schools and special districts, based on their mill levies. For a tax rate breakdown by district, the Treasurer's page says to call the Assessor's office.

When are Apache County property taxes due and when are they late?

Apache County property tax is paid in two halves: October 1 and March 1. The first half is delinquent if unpaid after November 1 at 5:00 p.m., and the second half after May 1 at 5:00 p.m., according to both the Treasurer's page and A.R.S. 42-18052.

  • If the whole year's tax is $100 or less, all of it is due October 1 and becomes delinquent after December 31 at 5:00 p.m.
  • If a delinquency date lands on a weekend or holiday, it moves to 5:00 p.m. on the next business day.
  • Delinquent accounts bear interest at 16% a year, prorated monthly, per the county.
  • Tax notices are mailed whether or not your lender pays through escrow, and not receiving one does not excuse late payment.

The sample math is simple. A bill of $1,200 for the year would be $600 on October 1 and $600 on March 1. That is only an illustration, because actual bills depend on the assessed value and the district rates for your parcel.

How can I pay Apache County property tax?

You can pay by mail, online with a card, or in person at the Treasurer's counter in St. Johns. The county encourages mailed payments and asks that checks be made out to the Apache County Treasurer.

  • Mail without a coupon goes to Apache County Treasurer, PO Box 699, St. Johns, AZ 85936.
  • Online payment with a credit or debit card runs through the county's property tax payment portal.
  • In person payments are taken at 75 West Cleveland during counter hours.

The Treasurer also offers an online tax account search. Run it for your parcel before a sale so you know exactly what is owed.

How do I challenge an Apache County valuation?

Start with a written petition to the Assessor. Under A.R.S. 42-16051, an owner who believes a property was valued too high may file the petition on the state form within 60 days after the assessor mailed the notice of valuation. The postmark date counts as the filing date.

The petition has to give the owner's opinion of the property's full cash value and support it. The statute names three ways to do that: an income approach, a market approach that cites at least one comparable property or the sale of your own property, or a cost approach based on the cost to build plus the land value.

If you miss the Assessor deadline, the county says you can still appeal the full cash value to the Arizona Tax Court before December 15 of the valuation year. The county asks you not to send those papers to the Assessor's office. The Assessor's site also offers paperless notices through its EagleWeb parcel database, using the key code on the Annual Notice of Value.

What if property tax goes unpaid in Apache County?

Unpaid property tax can end in a tax lien sale. The Treasurer explains that Arizona lets the county treasurer sell a delinquent lien at public auction, and Apache County lists liens for sale online for an auction held each February.

The Treasurer's page describes investors who may bid on the lien interest rate or bid up a premium, and notes that many buy to foreclose on the lien or to earn a high interest rate. It also links pages on certificates of purchase, redemption, and the foreclosure process.

The county posted a public notice of a tax lien auction for 2024 delinquent taxes on February 3, 2026. If you own a house with unpaid tax, you can ask the Treasurer for the payoff, then decide whether to pay, redeem or sell before the lien moves forward.

What should an Apache County seller check about tax before closing?

Check the balance first, then the districts, then who pays what at closing. Unpaid tax can hold up any sale, so settle the numbers early.

  • Ask the Assessor for the tax rates by district form, which shows the levies on your parcel.
  • Check whether your parcel appears on the Treasurer's tax lien lists, and read the Treasurer's redemption page if it does.
  • Confirm the owner of record, since notices go to the address on file. The Assessor has an address change request form.

The Assessor charges $1.00 per page for copies picked up, $1.50 per page mailed, and $300 for a data set, which can matter if you need records for a sale.

What is Apache County, Arizona, and who lives there?

Apache County is a long, narrow rectangle on Arizona's northeastern edge, organized in 1879 with St. Johns as its county seat. Its area is 11,218 square miles. The county has the largest share of Indian reservation land of any U.S. county, 68.34 percent of its area, and includes the Navajo Nation, the Fort Apache Indian Reservation and a Zuni Indian Reservation holding.

Wikipedia reports 66,021 residents at the 2020 census and a 2025 estimate of 64,445. The population peaked at 71,518 in 2010. In 2020, the county had 22,103 households, with a median age of 38.3 years. Eagar is the largest town, followed in the 2010 ranking by Chinle, Fort Defiance, St. Johns and Window Rock.

The incorporated places are the city of St. Johns and the towns of Eagar and Springerville, and most other named communities are census-designated places. If your parcel sits on or near reservation land, ask the Assessor and the Treasurer how it is assessed and billed before you set a price or a closing date, because this guide does not cover those cases.

When are Apache County property taxes due?

Apache County property tax is due in two halves, October 1 and March 1. The first half is delinquent after November 1 at 5:00 p.m. and the second after May 1 at 5:00 p.m.

What interest rate does Apache County charge on late property tax?

The county says delinquent accounts bear interest at 16% a year, prorated monthly. Check your parcel with the Treasurer for the amount owed.

How long do I have to appeal my Apache County assessment?

You have 60 days after the Assessor mailed your notice of valuation to file a petition under A.R.S. 42-16051. After that, the county says you can still go to the Arizona Tax Court before December 15 of the valuation year.

Where do I send my Apache County property tax payment?

Send it to Apache County Treasurer, PO Box 699, St. Johns, AZ 85936 if you have no coupon, or to the Houston, Texas box printed on the coupon if you do. You can also pay online or at 75 West Cleveland.

Can I sell an Apache County house with unpaid taxes?

Yes. Get the payoff from the Treasurer and settle it at closing or before. If a lien has been sold to an investor, ask the Treasurer about redemption.

Who handles property tax in Santa Cruz County, Arizona?

Congress Drive, Room 104, in Nogales, open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Mail goes to PO Box 1150, Nogales, AZ 85628, and checks are made out to the Santa Cruz County Treasurer. The Assessor controls value, legal class, exemptions and the mailing address printed on your bill.

Santa Cruz is the smallest county in Arizona by area, with 1,238 square miles, and it sits on the Mexican border. It was formed on March 15, 1899 out of Pima County and takes its name from the Santa Cruz River. Nogales is the county seat and the only city, Patagonia is the only incorporated town, and Rio Rico, Tubac, Sonoita and Amado are among the unincorporated communities. Two sellers in the same county can therefore deal with the same offices while living in very different places, from a border city lot in Nogales to a ranch parcel near Elgin.

Your bill adds up the rates of every jurisdiction that taxes your parcel: the county, your school district, your fire district and other special districts. The Treasurer explains that primary taxes pay operating costs and secondary taxes pay for special districts, bonds and voter-approved overrides. Primary tax is limited value times the assessment ratio times the primary rate divided by $100, and secondary tax follows the same pattern. Owner-occupied homes also get a State Aid to Education credit against the school primary tax, and a countywide Fire District Assistance tax under ARS 48-807 appears on every taxable parcel.

When are Santa Cruz County property taxes due and what happens if they are late?

Bills above $100 split into two installments. The first is due October 1 and delinquent if postmarked or received after 5:00 p.m. on November 1. The second is due March 1 and delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on May 1. A bill of $100 or less is due with the first installment. If you pay both installments in full before 5:00 p.m. on December 31, the interest on the first installment is waived. Statements for the current year go out in mid-September with a coupon for each installment, and that is the only statement you receive unless you fall behind.

Once a deadline passes, interest starts at 16 percent a year, prorated monthly at 1.333 percent whether you pay on the first or last day of the month. A $5 penalty applies to taxes still unpaid when January arrives. The county also warns that partial payment of delinquent tax liens is not allowed, so the minimum it accepts is the tax, interest and fees for a delinquent installment. For the date today, November 15, 2026, the first installment is already delinquent and the second comes due March 1, 2027.

Agriculture here leans on forage, hay and cattle, and the county has three border crossings, all in Nogales. A seller whose house is valued near $233,000 will see a bill built on the limited value, not on that headline figure, so read your own notice.

How do I pay a Santa Cruz County property tax bill?

You can pay online, by phone, by mail or in person. The county’s card vendor, Point&Pay, charges $3.95 on debit cards, 2.5 percent on credit card payments over $100 and $2.00 on credit payments below that. An electronic check costs $2.50. The Treasurer receives none of this and is barred by law from charging a processing fee. Allow three to four business days for an online payment to post. To see what you owe for the current year, search the parcel on the county’s property information site and open the taxes tab. For prior years, call the Treasurer at 520-375-7580, because extra charges may not show on the online tab. If you have a mortgage, the Treasurer supplies tax statements to mortgage and tax service companies on request, and you may also get an information statement as a courtesy. The Treasurer has also posted a notice that some bills carry installment amounts that need correcting while the full-year amount is right, so check the posted parcel list if your halves look odd.

How do I appeal a Santa Cruz County valuation?

File a Petition for Review of Real Property Valuation, Form 82130, with the Assessor. The Assessor mails notices of valuation by March 1, and state law gives you 60 days from the mailing date. The county FAQ points to the period from March 1 through April 29, and petitions are available at the Assessor’s office. Under ARS 42-16051, your petition must give your opinion of full cash value and back it with the income, market or cost approach.

The Assessor’s office also handles mailing address changes, so ask them to update it when you sell. The Assessor’s number is 520-375-8030. If the Assessor denies your petition, the next step is the County Board of Equalization, then court, within the deadlines printed on the decision.

Who qualifies for a Santa Cruz County property tax exemption?

The county lists exemptions for qualifying widows, widowers and disabled persons. You must apply each year between January 1 and the last working day of February, and first-time applicants must apply in person. Someone holding a power of attorney may file for another person with a copy of the power of attorney and photo ID. Each exemption has its own qualifications, so call the Assessor at 520-375-8030. State law also covers disabled veterans in ARS 42-11111.

The statute lists conveying title to another owner as an event that ends the exemption, so a seller should tell the Assessor after closing. A person who moves to a new primary residence has 60 days to file a transfer form with the assessor in that home’s county.

What happens when Santa Cruz County taxes go unpaid?

The county sells a lien for the unpaid tax at its delinquent tax lien sale, which it holds in February. The 2026 sale was held online on February 10, 2026. Investors bid the interest rate down from 16 percent in 1 percent steps, and a zero percent bid is allowed. The county says that after three years from the sale date, the lien purchaser can foreclose and acquire the property. The county treats this as a sale of the lien and not of the home.

A seller should settle the tax and any lien before closing. Call the Treasurer for a payoff figure, using 520-375-7980 for lien questions and 520-375-7580 for prior-year balances, and give it to the title or escrow company.

  • Ask whether either installment is open and whether any parcel interest has accrued.
  • Ask the Assessor to change the mailing address and cancel any exemption once title passes.

A house in Nogales, Rio Rico or Patagonia is taxed by the same county office, though the district rates that make up the bill differ by address.

Can I avoid interest on the first installment?

Interest runs at 16 percent a year, prorated at 1.333 percent a month, and a $5 penalty is added for taxes unpaid when January arrives. Unpaid taxes can be sold as a lien at the February tax lien sale.

Where do I pay property tax in person in Santa Cruz County?

At the Treasurer’s office, 2150 N. Congress Drive, Room 104, Nogales, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. You may also mail a check to PO Box 1150, Nogales, AZ 85628, or pay online or by phone with the vendor’s fees.

Can a veteran get a property tax exemption in Santa Cruz County?

State law in ARS 42-11111 provides exemptions for veterans with qualifying disability ratings. Ask the Santa Cruz County Assessor at 520-375-8030 whether you qualify and how to apply, and note that the county’s exemption filing window runs from January 1 to the last working day of February.

Who handles property tax in La Paz County, Arizona?

Two county offices split the work. The La Paz County Assessor values property and keeps ownership, parcel maps, exemptions, mobile homes and business personal property. The La Paz County Treasurer mails the bills and collects the money. The Assessor does not set tax rates, issue bills, or collect or refund taxes, so a question about an amount due goes to the Treasurer and a question about value goes to the Assessor.

  • Treasurer: 1112 Joshua Avenue, Suite 203, Parker, AZ 85344. Open Monday through Thursday, 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., closed Fridays.
  • Assessor: 1112 Joshua Avenue, Suite 204, Parker, AZ 85344, phone 928-669-6165.
  • Recorder: records deeds and answers fee questions at 928-669-6136.

The Assessor gets deed information from the Recorder and permit information from La Paz County Community Development, the Town of Parker and the Town of Quartzsite. A house that gains a room or loses a roof without a permit can still show up on the roll later, so keep your permit paperwork in the sale file.

What kind of county is La Paz County for a home seller?

La Paz County is a large, thinly settled county on Arizona's western edge with a small tax base. It covers 4,514 square miles, had 16,557 residents in the 2020 census, and its seat is Parker, the largest town. Quartzsite is the only other incorporated town. The Colorado River Indian Reservation lies in the western part of the county.

Voters created La Paz County in 1983 by separating the northern part of Yuma County, and it is the only Arizona county formed after statehood. Census figures show 13,457 housing units in 2020, of which 45.2% were vacant, and 71.8% of occupied homes were owner-occupied. Mobile homes are part of the local housing stock, and the Assessor's office keeps mobile home records.

The Assessor's FAQ explains one local wrinkle. The office updates mobile home ownership from Motor Vehicle Division title records, and it cannot change the owner on the roll until the new title is issued. If the old owner is still on the title, the old owner still gets the notice of value and the tax bill. Before you sell a mobile home, confirm the title has moved.

When are La Paz County property taxes due in 2026 and 2027?

Half of the tax is due on October 1 and the other half on the following March 1, under A.R.S. 42-18052. The Treasurer's notice for the 2026 roll gives these dates and a 6:00 p.m. delinquency hour.

DateWhat happens
October 1, 2026First half due. Bills were mailed September 11.
November 2, 2026, 6:00 p.m.First half delinquent. This date has passed.
December 31, 2026Last day to pay the full year and avoid interest.
March 1, 2027Second half due.
May 4, 2027, 6:00 p.m.Second half delinquent.

Source: La Paz County Treasurer. Postmarked payments are accepted, and the smallest accepted payment is $10 or 10% of the tax due, whichever is greater.

If you owe the first half and have not paid it, interest is already running. Paying the whole year by December 31 stops further interest under A.R.S. 42-18053, so a seller who closes in December can clear it at the table.

How much interest does La Paz County charge on late tax?

Unpaid taxes bear interest at 16% a year, simple, from the delinquency date, and a fraction of a month counts as a whole month. That rate comes from A.R.S. 42-18053. The Treasurer states the same 16%, prorated monthly from the first day of the month until paid.

  • No interest is collected if the delinquency came from an error by the assessor or treasurer.
  • No interest is collected if the full-year tax is paid on or before December 31 of the tax year.
  • The treasurer may waive interest and penalties once per property for a delinquency in the year after a mortgage or deed of trust is released, if the board of supervisors approves.

Ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure good through your expected closing date. Parcel lookup and card payments run through the Treasurer's website. Card payments carry a convenience fee of $4.00 on a Visa debit card or 2.55% on a credit card, and the jurisdiction code to give by phone is 1312.

How do you appeal a La Paz County valuation?

File a petition with the County Assessor within 60 days after the Assessor mailed your notice of value. That deadline is in A.R.S. 42-16051, and a postmark counts as the filing date. Notices go out each year to the owner of record, and the county tells owners that only the full cash value or the property class can be appealed.

The petition has to state your opinion of full cash value and give substantial information backing it. The statute names three methods: the income approach, the market approach (with at least one comparable property or the sale of the subject property), and the cost approach. A recent arm's-length sale of your own house is the strongest comparable you can offer.

The limited property value is separate. The Assessor's notice page explains that Proposition 117 caps growth in limited property value at 5% a year, with exceptions listed in A.R.S. Title 42, Chapter 13, Article 7. Because bills run on limited value, a jump in full cash value does not always raise your tax by the same amount.

What tax relief exists for La Paz County homeowners?

The Assessor's FAQ describes two programs, and the office can give you the current income and value limits. Call 928-669-6165 before you list.

  • Exemption for widows, widowers and totally disabled persons age 17 or over. You must live in Arizona, meet income requirements, and stay under an indexed assessed-value limit. A disability claim needs a physician's certification that the disability is total and permanent.
  • Senior Property Valuation Protection, often called the senior freeze. It freezes limited property value for three years. You must be 65 at the time of application, use the home as your primary Arizona residence, and meet income rules.

The FAQ adds that a value can jump when a buyer takes over a home whose prior owner held a senior freeze. A buyer should expect a first notice of value that looks higher than the seller's. The Assessor's page also lists a rental registration form and points rental owners to the state's online lodging marketplace registration for short-term rentals.

How does unpaid tax affect a sale in La Paz County?

Property tax is a lien on the house, and under A.R.S. 42-17153 it attaches on January 1 of the tax year. It outranks other liens except those held by the state and tax liens from other years. It stays until the taxes, penalties, charges and interest are paid, a tax sale vests title in a buyer, or a certificate of removal and abatement is issued. A buyer's title company will therefore expect that the current year and any back years are paid from your proceeds.

The deed itself has a few requirements. A deed that transfers title must carry a sworn affidavit of property value from seller and buyer under A.R.S. 11-1133, and the recorder must refuse a deed without it unless it carries an exemption notation. The La Paz County Recorder lists the document rules online: paper 8 1/2 inches wide and 11 to 14 inches long, a two-inch top margin on the first page, original ink signatures, and the right fee. Ask the Recorder's office for the current fee schedule at 928-669-6136.

Selling a house with tax due is routine when the numbers are clear. Get the payoff from the Treasurer, confirm the owner of record with the Assessor, and give both numbers to the title company.

More questions about La Paz County, AZ Property Tax Guide

Are La Paz County property taxes still open to pay in November 2026?

Yes. The first half became delinquent on November 2, 2026 at 6:00 p.m., so interest of 16% a year is accruing on that half. Paying the full year on or before December 31, 2026 stops interest from running under A.R.S. 42-18053. The second half is due March 1, 2027 and is delinquent after May 4, 2027.

Where do I pay La Paz County property tax?

Pay the County Treasurer at 1112 Joshua Avenue, Suite 203, Parker, Arizona 85344, by mail or in person, or pay online or by phone. The office is open Monday through Thursday, 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., and closed Fridays. Card payments add a $4.00 fee on Visa debit or 2.55% on credit cards.

How long do I have to appeal my La Paz County notice of value?

You have 60 days from the date the Assessor mailed the notice. File a petition with the County Assessor stating your opinion of full cash value and the information that supports it. A.R.S. 42-16051 accepts the postmark as the filing date.

Does La Paz County have a senior property tax freeze?

Yes. The Assessor administers Senior Property Valuation Protection, which freezes limited property value for three years. The owner must be 65 at application, live in the home as a primary Arizona residence, and meet income limits. Call the Assessor at 928-669-6165 for the form and current limits.

Can I sell a La Paz County house that still has tax due?

Yes. The tax lien attaches on January 1 of the tax year and is paid from sale proceeds at closing. Get a payoff amount from the Treasurer for your closing date, since interest runs monthly on delinquent amounts, and give it to the title company.

Graham County by the numbers

Where do Graham County property owners pay their taxes?

Property tax in Graham County is paid to the Graham County Treasurer in Safford, which collects on behalf of all nineteen taxing authorities in the county. The Treasurer's office is in the General Services Building at 921 Thatcher Blvd.,.

  • In person: the Treasurer's Office accepts cash, checks, and credit or debit cards.
  • By mail: P.O. Box 747, Safford, AZ 85548.
  • Drop box: in the east parking lot of the General Services Building.
  • Online: through Point and Pay, which adds a convenience fee of 2.45 percent for credit cards (minimum $2.00), $1.50 for an electronic check, or $3.95 for a debit card.

Call the Treasurer at 928-428-3440 to confirm an amount due, and the Assessor at 928-428-2828 for valuation questions. The Treasurer's tax search is refreshed hourly during business days and shows balances and lien redemption amounts.

What are the Graham County property tax due dates?

The first half is due October 1 and goes delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 1, and the second half is due March 1 and goes delinquent after 5 p.m. on May 1. Bills are mailed in September on a single statement with two stubs.

When November 1 or May 1 lands on a weekend or holiday, delinquency moves to 5 p.m. on the next business day. In 2026 November 1 was a Sunday, so the first half of this year's bill went delinquent after 5 p.m. on Monday, November 2. That deadline has passed. The second half is due March 1, 2027. May 1, 2027 falls on a Saturday, which puts the delinquency cutoff at 5 p.m. on Monday, May 3.

The county accepts partial payments, monthly or semi-monthly if you like. A partial payment does not stop interest from building on the past-due balance.

What happens if you do not receive a Graham County tax bill?

You still owe the tax and the interest. The Graham County Treasurer states that failure to receive a statement is not a legal reason to waive interest, and A.R.S. 42-18054 says the same about liability for tax, interest, fees and penalties.

If no statement has arrived by October 1, call the Treasurer's Office at 928-428-3440 for the amount. Check the parcel number and description on each statement against your own records before you pay, so a payment is not applied to the wrong property. Owners with a mortgage should confirm that the lender requested the bill. Many lenders pull tax information directly from the county, and the owner then receives an informational postcard. Lenders that do not make the request leave the statement to go to the owner.

How is Graham County property valued for tax?

The Assessor must mail a Notice of Valuation to every owner of record before March 1 each year. Since Proposition 117 took effect for tax year 2015, the Limited Property Value is the only value used to figure the tax, and it can rise no more than 5 percent per year.

That detail shapes an appeal. Your tax rests on the Limited Property Value, but only the Full Cash Value, which reflects market value, can be appealed. The limited figure comes from the prior year's value or a formula in state law, so there is nothing to argue about in it directly.

Rates are the other half of the bill. Each of the taxing authorities that levies on your parcel, from the county to your school district, sets its own rate, and A.R.S. 42-17151 requires those levies to be fixed on or before the third Monday in August. The Treasurer's page for current-year rates lists rates by taxing authority and combined rates by area. Call the Treasurer's Office with questions about balances and due dates, and the Assessor's Office for questions about values.

How do you appeal a Graham County property valuation?

Petition the Assessor for review within 60 days of the notice date printed on the front of your Notice of Valuation. A.R.S. 42-16051 sets that 60-day limit and asks you to state your opinion of full cash value along with information that supports it.

Graham County lists the state forms on its Assessment and Appeals page:

  • DOR 82130R for residential property.
  • DOR 82130 for commercial, industrial, vacant land and agricultural property.
  • DOR 82131 for multiple parcels, and DOR 82130NC for a Notice of Change.
  • DOR 82130AA if you want an agent to act for you.
  • DOR 82300 and its supplements, for commercial appeals based on income and expense statements.

If the Assessor's answer does not settle the matter, the Arizona Department of Revenue says you may take the appeal to the Board of Equalization, the Tax Court, or both. It also allows you to file your original appeal directly with the Tax Court. The decision letter from the Assessor states the next deadline, so read it the day it arrives.

Which relief programs can lower a Graham County tax bill?

Arizona law offers exemptions for widows and widowers, people with a total and permanent disability, and honorably discharged veterans with a disability, plus a Senior Freeze, and the County Assessor runs each one. The Arizona Department of Revenue explains that the exemptions reduce taxable value up to a set dollar amount and that household income limits apply to every individual exemption.

Three points from the state's guidance are useful when you plan a sale:

  • You can claim only one individual exemption, even if you fit more than one category.
  • Changes to the veteran exemption apply to tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, and a new veteran application goes to the Assessor between the first Monday in January and March 1.
  • The Senior Freeze fixes the valuation of a primary residence for a renewable three years for owners who meet age and income rules. Taxes are still levied at the district rate.

Dollar limits change every year. Ask the Graham County Assessor at 928-428-2828 for this year's amounts and forms.

What happens when Graham County taxes go unpaid?

The Treasurer sells the delinquent taxes to an investor at a lien sale held each February. The 2024 taxes, for example, were offered at the auction on February 25, 2026. Bidders compete on the lowest interest rate they will accept, and the winning bidder receives a registered Certificate of Purchase.

The parcel list is posted outside the Treasurer's office, advertised in the Eastern Arizona Courier, and updated weekly in February on the county website. Buyers of a lien must also take assignment of any older outstanding certificates on the parcel. If you owe back tax, call 928-428-3440 for the exact payoff.

What changes when a Graham County house sells?

The title company handling the sale normally decides who pays the current year's tax, and the statement usually follows the deed into the new owner's name about a year after the sale is recorded. Graham County's guide says current-year taxes may not even be assessed yet depending on the closing date.

Mobile homes that have a title are billed as personal property. The tax record changes only when a new title is issued in the buyer's name, and signing the back of the old title does not update the tax roll. Sellers of a titled mobile home should finish the title transfer so the next bill goes to the right person.

What is Graham County like for sellers?

Graham County was created on March 10, 1881, and Safford is both the county seat and the largest city. The seat moved to Solomonville in 1883 and returned to Safford in 1915. The towns are Thatcher and Pima. The county includes part of the San Carlos Apache Indian Reservation, Eastern Arizona College, and the Mount Graham International Observatory in the Pinaleno Mountains.

Census Bureau figures show a 2025 population of 40,157 and 14,645 housing units. The median owner-occupied home was valued at $212,000 for 2020 through 2024, owners occupy 73.1 percent of homes, and median household income was $67,325. The median age was 33.8 at the 2020 census, which makes this a younger county than its neighbor Gila County.

More questions about Graham County, AZ Property Tax Guide

How much interest does Graham County charge on late property tax?

The rate is 16 percent simple interest per year, prorated monthly on the first day of each month. Paying the full year by December 31 avoids interest, and a missing statement does not waive it.

Can I make partial payments on my Graham County taxes?

Yes. The Treasurer accepts partial payments monthly, semi-monthly or on your own schedule. Interest continues to build on whatever past-due balance remains.

What is the deadline to appeal a Graham County valuation?

You have 60 days from the notice date on the front of your Notice of Valuation to petition the Assessor. The Notice is mailed before March 1 each year.

Is there a fee to pay Graham County property tax online?

Yes. The service provider, Point and Pay, charges 2.45 percent for credit cards with a $2.00 minimum, $1.50 for an electronic check and $3.95 for a debit card. Paying at the office, by mail or in the drop box avoids that fee.

Who do I call about a Graham County tax balance?

Call the Graham County Treasurer's Office at 928-428-3440 for balances, due dates and payment options. Call the Assessor at 928-428-2828 for values, exemptions and appeal forms.
